newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak April CPI steady, big falls unlikely in 97.
newsitem.headline: Slovak April CPI steady, big falls unlikely in 97.

text.p: Slovak consumer inflation was steady in April at one of the lowest levels in central Europe, but analysts said on Tuesday they did not expect a radical slowdown in the rate throughout the year.
The Slovak Statistical Bureau (SUSR) released data showing CPI rising 0.5 percent month-on-month in April, putting prices up 6.5 percent over the same month in 1996.
Inflation rose 0.5 percent in March 1997 against February, with the annual rate standing at 6.3 percent.
Some analysts said the CPI had shown a favourable trend so far this year, attributing the slight acceleration in April to the effect of last year's increase in pensions.

"The CPI shows a positive trend, but we don't expect a rapid slowdown in the near future since we have already come close to the so-called core inflation, which is natural for any economic growth," said Juraj Rencko, chief economic analyst at the Slovak Academy of Science.
"Though at this point further cuts in CPI would be difficult, I expect the annual average rate to be at around the same level as in 1996," Rencko said.
The average annual inflation stood at 5.8 percent in 1996.
The 1997 budget is based on an assumption that the average inflation rate will not exceed six percent.

The National Bank of Slovakia (NBS) has set its target for annual 1997 inflation at up to 5.8 percent, but it based its projection on GDP growth of around five percent, compared with the budget prediction at least six percent growth in 1997.
Martin Barto, an analyst at ING Barings, said inflation at above the targeted levels was not so far a warning signal, but he said a 0.5 percent month-on-month increase was higher than expected.
"It is not alarming yet, but the trend must be very closely watched and analysed to find the reason behind the faster than expected month-on-month increase," Barto said.

The SUSR did not provide details of the April CPI. It only said the fastest growing items on the month-on-month base were health care (+4.0 percent) and household costs, electrical energy and gas (+1.5 percent).
On the year-on-year base, education rose by 11.2 percent, followed by health care with a 9.6 percent increase, shoes and clothes, up 7.7 percent, and food and non-alcoholic drinks, up 7.5 percent.
Barto forecast the annual inflation rate would be slighlty above six percent. "But, based on the current month-on-month trend, I would say it will be closer to 6.5 percent than to 6.0," he said
